nodes.title: Find where the item sits

anchor.snippet: function locate(items: Item[], id: string, parents: number[] = []): { parents: number[]; index: number } | null {

nodes.why: Every operation needs the same two facts: which sibling list holds the item and where in it. One search that returns both keeps the operations short.
nodes.alternative: Keep a parent pointer on each item.
nodes.tradeoff: Parent pointers make lookups cheap but must be fixed on every move, and they make the tree harder to copy immutably.

nodes.title: Replace one sibling list, copy only its path

anchor.snippet: function withSiblings(items: Item[], parents: number[], change: (siblings: Item[]) => Item[]): Item[] {

nodes.why: Copying the lists along the path and reusing everything else gives a new tree for React without mutating the old one.
nodes.alternative: Deep-clone the tree and mutate the clone.
nodes.tradeoff: A clone is simple to write, but it copies the whole tree on every keystroke and gives every item a new identity.

nodes.title: Indent under the previous sibling

anchor.snippet: function indent(items: Item[], id: string): Item[] {

nodes.why: An outliner nests an item under the one above it, so the item joins the end of its previous sibling's children. A first child has nothing above it at its level, so it stays.
nodes.alternative: Make the item the first child of its previous sibling.
nodes.tradeoff: Putting it first reorders the previous sibling's children, which a reader does not expect from one Tab.

nodes.title: Outdent to right after the parent

anchor.snippet: function outdent(items: Item[], id: string): Item[] {

nodes.why: The item becomes its parent's next sibling, and its later siblings stay where they were, so one Shift+Tab moves exactly one item.
nodes.alternative: Take the later siblings along as the item's children.
nodes.tradeoff: Some outliners do that; it keeps the visual order but changes several items at once, which this task does not ask for.

nodes.title: Focus follows the id once, after the change
nodes.why: An item that moves to a new list is a new input element. Focusing by id in an effect after the update finds the element wherever it rendered, and clearing the id afterwards leaves focus alone on later edits.
nodes.tradeoff: In the handler the moved input does not exist yet, so focus would land on the old, unmounted element.

nodes.title: Escape is the way out
nodes.why: Taking Tab for indentation removes the usual way to leave the outline, so Escape moves focus to the button after it.
nodes.alternative: Leave Tab to the browser and indent with another shortcut.
nodes.tradeoff: That avoids the trap, but outliners users know indent with Tab, and the task asks for it.
